title: Sleep, Insomnia & the Psychology of Rest
description: Explore sleep pressure accumulated through waking through dialogue, evidence and psychological reasoning.

lessons.title: Why an early bedtime isn't enough
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of sleep pressure accumulated through waking.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), A Two Process Model of Sleep Regulation; NICE insomnia guidance.
nodes.scenario: Nora woke just after noon and is trying to sleep at nine in the evening.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I've been in bed an hour and I'm wide awake.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: When did you get up this morning?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: After twelve. I thought an early night would reset the schedule.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Are you sleepy, or mainly worried about tomorrow?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Mostly worried. I'm checking the clock because I need eight hours.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Going to bed early doesn't guarantee the body is ready for sleep.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Nora may be experiencing a separate persistent sleep disorder that needs assessment.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Nora may have relatively little sleep pressure at the chosen bedtime, compounded by sleep-related worry. nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Sleep is regulated partly by homeostatic pressure accumulated during wakefulness and by circadian timing. An early bedtime after waking late may not match either process. Watching the clock and trying hard to sleep can then make the bed a cue for monitoring rather than settling.

Insomnia has multiple causes, and persistent difficulty merits appropriate assessment. Sleep needs and health circumstances vary.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), A Two Process Model of Sleep Regulation; NICE insomnia guidance.

nodes.title: Try a different response
nodes.prompt: The goal is to improve the situation without pretending that you can read the person's mind.
nodes.explanation: A proportionate response deals with the actual situation: Use a sustainable wake-time plan and seek evidence-based support if the difficulty persists. Its value does not depend on the other person accepting an interpretation of their motives.
nodes.counterexample: Some situations require independent support or safer channels rather than another direct conversation. Insomnia has multiple causes, and persistent difficulty merits appropriate assessment. Sleep needs and health circumstances vary.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), A Two Process Model of Sleep Regulation; NICE insomnia guidance.

options.label: Both viewpoints matter for understanding the exchange, but neither alone establishes the full cause; address the observable concern as well.

nodes.title: One distinction to keep
nodes.prompt: Fill the missing word: An explanation of what a behaviour might achieve is a working ______, not a proven fact.
nodes.explanation: A hypothesis is an explanation that can be revised when observations fail to support it. This keeps psychological reasoning useful rather than turning it into confident mind-reading.
nodes.counterexample: Insomnia has multiple causes, and persistent difficulty merits appropriate assessment. Sleep needs and health circumstances vary.
nodes.sources: Borbély (1982), A Two Process Model of Sleep Regulation; NICE insomnia guidance.
